segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that very time some people were present who told him about the Galileans whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He answered them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Do you think that these Galileans were worse sinners than all the other Galileans because they have suffered these things?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No, I tell you; but unless you turn back, you will all perish likewise.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Or those eighteen on whom the tower in Siloam fell and killed them—do you think they were worse debtors than all the other people living in Jerusalem?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: No, I tell you; but unless you turn back, you will all perish in the same way.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Then he told this parable:

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “A man had a fig tree planted in his vineyard, and he came looking for fruit on it and found none.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: So he said to the vinedresser, ‘Look, for three years now I have been coming to look for fruit on this fig tree and finding none. Cut it down! Why should it use up the ground as well?’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But he answered him, ‘Sir, leave it this year too, until I dig around it and put manure on it.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then if it bears fruit in the coming year—but if not, you can cut it down.’”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He was teaching in one of the synagogues on the Sabbath.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And there was a woman there who for eighteen years had had a disabling spirit; she was bent over and unable to straighten up fully.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: When Jesus saw her, he called to her and said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Woman, you are released from your disability,”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and he laid his hands on her. At once she was made straight, and she began glorifying God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But the synagogue leader, indignant that Jesus had healed on the Sabbath, responded by saying to the crowd,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “There are six days on which one ought to work; so come and be healed on those days, and not on the Sabbath day.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The Lord answered him,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Hypocrites! Does not each of you on the Sabbath untie his ox or his donkey from the manger and lead it away to water it?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And this woman, a daughter of Abraham whom Satan has bound for eighteen long years—ought she not to have been untied from this bond on the Sabbath day?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: As he said these things, all his opponents were put to shame, and the whole crowd rejoiced at all the glorious things being done by him.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “What is the kingdom of God like, and to what shall I compare it?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It is like a mustard seed that a man took and sowed in his garden; it grew and became a tree, and the birds of the sky nested in its branches.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And again he said,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “To what shall I compare the kingdom of God?

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: It is like leaven that a woman took and hid in three measures of flour until all of it was leavened.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He went on through town after town and village after village, teaching and making his way to Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Someone said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Lord, are only a few being saved?”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Strive to enter through the narrow door, because many, I tell you, will try to enter and will not be able,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: once the master of the house has risen and shut the door and you begin to stand outside and knock at the door, saying, ‘Lord, open up for us!’ And he will answer you, ‘I do not know you, or where you are from.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Then you will begin to say, ‘We ate and drank in your presence, and you taught in our streets.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: But he will say to you, ‘I do not know where you are from. Get away from me, all you workers of wrongdoing!’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: In that place there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, when you see Abraham and Isaac and Jacob and all the prophets in the kingdom of God, but yourselves being thrown out.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And people will come from east and west and from north and south and will recline at table in the kingdom of God.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: And look, there are some who are last who will be first, and some who are first who will be last.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: At that very hour some Pharisees came up and said to him,

segments.speaker: other
segments.text: “Leave and go on from here, because Herod wants to kill you.”

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: He said to them,

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: “Go and tell that fox, ‘Look, I am casting out demons and performing healings today and tomorrow, and on the third day I reach my goal.’

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Nevertheless, I must go on my way today and tomorrow and the day after, because it cannot be that a prophet should perish outside Jerusalem.

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Jerusalem, Jerusalem, who kills the prophets and stones those sent to her—how often I wanted to gather your children the way a hen gathers her own brood under her wings, and you did not want it!

segments.speaker: Jesus
segments.text: Look, your house is left to you. And I tell you, you will certainly not see me until the time comes when you say, ‘Blessed is the one who comes in the name of the Lord!’”

notes.phrase: whose blood Pilate had mixed with their sacrifices
notes.note: The phrase implies that Pilate’s soldiers killed these Galilean pilgrims while they were offering sacrifices, which could only have happened at the temple in Jerusalem. Neither this incident nor the collapse of the tower in Siloam (verse 4) is recorded in any other surviving source. Both were evidently recent news that Jesus’s hearers knew.

The traditional rendering is “repent,” which most translations keep as an established term that includes a change of life. In current English, however, “repent” centers on feeling sorry. The Greek word in the Gospels carries the prophets’ call to “return” to God—a change of direction in mind and conduct—so “turn back” is used here.

The Greek word is literally “debtors,” and most translations paraphrase it as “offenders,” “sinners” or “more guilty.” Speaking of sin as a debt owed to God was a common Jewish idiom (compare the Lord’s Prayer), and it is parallel here to “sinners” in verse 2. The image is kept because the Greek has it.

notes.phrase: Then if it bears fruit in the coming year—but if not
notes.traditional: if it bears fruit next year, well and good; but if not
notes.note: The Greek sentence breaks off without stating what happens if the tree bears fruit. Most translations supply “well” or “fine.” The broken sentence is kept here; it is a natural feature of speech, and the unstated outcome is obvious. “In the coming year” could also be rendered more loosely as “in the future.”

The closing Greek phrase can be read with “straighten up” (she could not straighten up completely) or with “unable” (she could not straighten up at all). Interpreters and translations are divided, and the difference is one of degree. The first reading is followed here.

notes.traditional: loosed / set free from this bond
notes.note: Jesus uses the same verb for untying an ox or donkey (verse 15) and for releasing the woman, and sets it against Satan’s having “bound” her. Most modern translations have “untie” in verse 15 and “set free” here, which hides the repetition on which the argument turns. Likewise “ought” here answers the synagogue leader’s “ought” in verse 14, as it does in the Greek.

notes.phrase: the birds of the sky nested in its branches
notes.note: The image of a great tree in whose branches the birds nest is used in the Scriptures for a kingdom that shelters many nations (Ezekiel 17:23; 31:6; Daniel 4:12, 21). Hearers familiar with those passages would have caught the echo. Mustard is a garden herb that grows unusually large from a very small seed; calling it a “tree” serves that echo.

The measure is the saton (Hebrew seah). Three of them come to roughly forty liters of flour, enough bread for well over a hundred people. The quantity is deliberately enormous, matching the tree that grows from the mustard seed. “Leaven” was a piece of fermented dough kept back from an earlier batch, not packaged yeast.

notes.phrase: once the master of the house has risen
notes.note: The Greek syntax across verses 24–25 is loose. The edition translated here links the clause to verse 24: many will be unable to enter once the door has been shut. Many translations instead begin a new sentence at verse 25 (“When once the master of the house has risen … then you will begin to say …”). The overall sense is little affected.

Herod here is Herod Antipas, the ruler of Galilee and Perea who had executed John the Baptist. In Greek and Jewish usage the fox was a figure for craftiness, and sometimes for a petty creature in contrast to a lion. Which nuance dominates here is debated; either way the term is dismissive.

Older versions have “I shall be perfected”; modern ones vary between “I finish my course,” “I reach my goal” and similar. The verb means to be brought to an intended end or completion, not to become morally flawless. Most interpreters take it as pointing to Jesus’s death in Jerusalem (verse 33). “Today and tomorrow, and on the third day” is an idiom for a short, fixed period.

notes.phrase: your house is left to you
notes.traditional: your house is left to you desolate
notes.note: Many later manuscripts add “desolate,” probably under the influence of Jeremiah 22:5 or the parallel in Matthew 23:38 as commonly read. The earliest witnesses to Luke lack the word, and it is omitted here. “Your house” may refer to the temple or to the city and its people as a whole; the saying means it is abandoned to its own keeping.

candidates.reason: Recurs across Luke, Paul and John, where translations vary between “unrighteousness,” “injustice,” “wickedness” and “wrongdoing,” and the link with the δίκαιος word family is easily lost.
Covers illness, physical disability and weakness across the Gospels and Paul; the choice between “weakness,” “infirmity,” “sickness” and “disability” needs fixing by sense.
Translations split between “leaven” and “yeast” across the Gospels, 1 Corinthians 5 and Galatians 5, and the image should read the same everywhere.
The fixed phrase “weeping and gnashing of teeth” occurs seven times in Matthew and Luke and should be identical each time; “gnashing” versus “grinding” needs one decision.
Used for sinners as well as literal debtors (Matthew 6:12; 18:24; Romans 1:14; 8:12); whether to keep the debt image or paraphrase it should be decided once.
